text.p: Germany's Commerzbank AG on Tuesday forecast a further rise in operating earnings this year after declaring itself "completely satisfied" with results in the first two months of 1997.

The bank said net interest and commission income jumped by 20 percent in January and February compared with the year-earlier period. Operating profit before risk provisions rose by 21.6 percent to 626 million marks ($364.9 million).
"We are completely satisfied with our profit and loss accounts for January and February '97," said chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen.
Commerzbank had no immediate plans to raise capital and that its move to ask shareholders to authorise a capital increase was purely a precautionary measure, he said.
He also scoffed at recent market speculation that the bank may become subject to a takeover bid, saying its strong share price performance had made it prohibitively expensive.

Kohlhaussen told the bank's annual news conference that its market capitalisation had trebled to more than 18 billion marks in the last four years. "Can you name me anyone who can afford that price?" he said.

Commerzbank's shares have surged 36.5 percent since the end of November to 46.30 marks on April 8, partly amid market talk that it may become one of several banks to face merger or takeover bids in Germany's overcrowded banking market.
Detailing its 1996 results, Commerzbank said a 24 percent jump in net profit to 1.21 billion marks last year stemmed from strong increases in net interest and commission income.
Those gains offset a 37 percent rise in risk provisions to 1.22 billion marks amid record corporate insolvencies in western Germany and a sharp rise in loan defaults.
Loan loss provisions for corporate clients were increased by almost 60 percent last year while provisions for retail customers rose by eight percent.
Kohlhaussen warned it was too early to expect a major improvement in risk provisions this year.
The bank also needed to make its domestic retail branch network more profitable by merging branches and concentrating back office duties in regional centres, he said.
Only then could it achieve its goal of a return on equity of 15 percent and a cost-income ratio of 60 to 62 percent in the medium term.
After-tax return on equity rose to 10.1 percent in 1996 from 9.3 percent while the cost-income ratio improved by falling to 65 percent from 70 percent.

Profit from own-account trade edged down to 450 million marks last year from 455 million, largely due to a 30 percent drop in income from currency trading. Income from trading in interest futures advanced to 274 million marks to 259 million.

Commerzbank has put Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG in the shadow by building Europe's largest office tower as its Frankfurt headquarters. But it has been less ambitious than its two rivals in investment banking, preferring to expand through organic growth rather than major acquisitions.

"We are not chasing fantasy prices in investment banking but decided at an early stage...to pursue this business under our own steam, with the centre of competence and strong bases in the important financial markets," Kohlhaussen said.
Commerzbank paid well under $200 million for Montgomery Asset Management, the U.S. firm it bought in March which has about eight billion dollars in assets under management, Kohlhaussen said.
He added that he did not expect further such acquisitions during 1997. ($ = 1.715 German Marks)
